metadata.scope: e_illyria (all 165 baronies across k_croatia, k_epirus, k_sicily, and k_venice)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_jajce.first_mention_attestation: 1396 AD (title 'conte de Jajce' of Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić)

morphemes.translation: egg (referring to the egg-shaped hill of the fortress)

b_jajce.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *jajce* ('egg'), after the egg-shaped hill on which the fortress stands; first attested in 1396 AD.

b_kljucnasani.first_mention_attestation: 1322 AD (charter of Ban Stjepan II Kotromanić)
b_kljucnasani.etymology_analysis: From Slavic *ključ* ('key'), denoting its strategic control of the Sana valley; first mentioned in 1322 AD.

b_greben.first_mention_attestation: 1192 AD (first mentioned in medieval sources as Greben)
b_greben.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *greben* ('ridge/crag'), referring to the rocky ridge above the Vrbas gorge; first attested in 1192 AD.

b_kotorvaros.first_mention_attestation: 1322 AD (medieval fortress Kotor in župa Vrbanja)
b_kotorvaros.etymology_analysis: From medieval fortress *Kotor* (first attested 1322 AD) plus Hungarian-derived *varoš* ('town').

b_sokol.first_mention_attestation: 1363 AD (siege by King Louis I of Hungary, defended by Vukac Hrvatinić)
b_sokol.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *sokol* ('falcon'), a common medieval Bosnian hillfort name; first attested in 1363 AD.

b_bihac.first_mention_attestation: 1260 AD (charter of King Béla IV of Hungary)

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly royal estate or island settlement

b_bihac.etymology_analysis: First mentioned on 26 February 1260 in a charter of King Béla IV as a town on the Island of St. Ladislav in the Una river.

b_krupa.first_mention_attestation: 13th century AD (fortress of Krupa first mentioned in 13th c.)

morphemes.translation: grain / groats or steep rocky bank / hail

b_krupa.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress Krupa on the Una river, first attested in the 13th century (replacing earlier župa Pset).

b_pset.first_mention_attestation: c. 949 AD (župa Pesenta in Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio)
b_pset.etymology_analysis: Early medieval Croatian župa Pset (*Pesenta*), first attested in *De Administrando Imperio* (c. 949 AD). Post-867 attestation.

b_visoki.first_mention_attestation: 1355 AD (charter of Ban Tvrtko I 'in castro nostro Visoka')
b_visoki.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *visok* ('high'), referring to the hilltop fortress on Visočica hill; first attested in 1355 AD.

b_prozor.first_mention_attestation: 1366 AD (charter of Ban Tvrtko I 'pod Prozorom u Rami')
b_prozor.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *prozor* ('window/lookout'), first attested in 1366 AD under Ban Tvrtko I.

b_vranduk.first_mention_attestation: 1410 AD (Ragusan complaint to King Sigismund mentioning Vranduk)
b_vranduk.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *braniti* ('to defend') / *branduk*; first attested in 1410 AD.

b_bobovac.first_mention_attestation: 1349 AD (first mentioned in a document during Ban Stjepan II's reign)
b_bobovac.etymology_analysis: Royal Bosnian fortress built under Ban Stjepan II Kotromanić, first attested in 1349 AD.

b_travnik.first_mention_attestation: 1463 AD (conquest by Sultan Mehmed II en route to Jajce)
b_travnik.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *trava* ('grass'), either 'grassy valley' or 'tax collector of travarina'; first attested in 1463 AD.

b_vhrbosna.first_mention_attestation: 1244 AD (cathedral church of St. Peter in Vrhbosna, charter of Béla IV)
b_vhrbosna.etymology_analysis: Slavic *Vrh-Bosna* ('upper reaches/peak of the Bosna'), first attested in 1244 AD.

b_olovo.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *olovo* ('lead'), named after its rich lead ore deposits; first attested in 1382 AD as Latin *Plumbum*.

b_kuclat.first_mention_attestation: 1346 AD (first mentioned in medieval Bosnian sources)

morphemes.translation: fortress name, possibly from Kušlatović family or Turkish/Slavic root

b_kuclat.etymology_analysis: Medieval rock fortress above the Jadar–Drinjača confluence, first attested in 1346 AD.

b_srebrenica.first_mention_attestation: 1376 AD (earliest reference to the name Srebrenica)
b_srebrenica.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *srebro* ('silver'), first attested in 1376 AD (near Roman silver-mining settlement *Domavia* / *Argentaria*).

historical_names.name: Domavia
historical_names.source: 2nd–3rd century AD (Roman municipium Domavia, mining center)
historical_names.notes: Roman mining municipium Domavia (modern Gradina/Sase near Srebrenica) operated in the 2nd–4th centuries AD.

b_rogatica.first_mention_attestation: 1425 AD (first mentioned in medieval Ragusan/Bosnian records)
b_rogatica.etymology_analysis: Derived from Slavic *rog* ('horn/spur') or personal name; first attested in 1425 AD near Borač Castle.

b_cres.first_mention_attestation: 77 AD (Crepsa in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia)
b_cres.etymology_analysis: From ancient Liburnian/Latin *Crepsa* (attested by Pliny the Elder, 77 AD), yielding Croatian *Cres* and Italian *Cherso*.

b_krk.first_mention_attestation: 1st century AD (Curicum in Pliny the Elder and Ptolemy)
b_krk.etymology_analysis: From Liburnian/Roman *Curicum* (1st century AD), becoming *Vecla* in Dalmatian and *Krk* in Croatian.

b_senj.etymology_analysis: Ancient Liburnian/Roman *Senia* (attested from 4th c. BC / 1st c. AD), Slavicized as *Senj* in the 7th–9th centuries.

b_brinje.first_mention_attestation: 1343 AD (castle Sokolac above Brinje first mentioned)
b_brinje.etymology_analysis: From Chakavian *brinja* ('juniper'); medieval Frankopan town below Sokolac castle, first attested in 1343 AD (near Roman *Monetium*).

historical_names.name: Monetium
historical_names.source: 1st century AD (Iapodian/Roman Monetium, Pliny/Strabo)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Iapodian/Roman settlement Monetium was located in the Brinje area.

b_rijeka.first_mention_attestation: 1281 AD (Flumen Sancti Viti / Reka in medieval charters)
b_rijeka.etymology_analysis: Croatian *Rijeka* / Italian *Fiume* ('river', referring to the Rječina), attested from the 13th century (1281 AD). Preceded by Roman/early medieval *Tarsatica* (Trsat, besieged by Franks in 799 AD).

historical_names.name: Tarsatica
historical_names.source: 1st century AD (Pliny's Tarsatica; Frankish Siege of Trsat 799 AD)
historical_names.notes: Roman Tarsatica (modern Trsat/Rijeka) was attested in the 1st century AD and in 799 AD.

historical_names.name: Tharsatica
historical_names.source: 1st century AD (Pliny's Tarsatica; Frankish Siege of Trsat 799 AD)
historical_names.notes: Roman Tarsatica (modern Trsat/Rijeka) was attested in the 1st century AD and in 799 AD.

b_kaseg.first_mention_attestation: 1263 AD (Kasezi / Gospić first mentioned in 13th century; Lika župa 949 AD)

morphemes.translation: a medieval Croatian noble/social group (kasegi) in Lika

b_kaseg.etymology_analysis: CK3 b_kaseg represents Kasezi (medieval Gospić, attested 1263 AD) in Lika (župa Lika attested 949 AD in DAI).

b_bag.first_mention_attestation: 1387 AD (medieval Bag, renamed Karlobag after Emperor Charles IV/Archduke Charles)
b_bag.etymology_analysis: First attested as *Bag* in 1387 AD (later *Karlobag*); preceded in antiquity by Liburnian/Roman *Vegium* (Pliny/Ptolemy).

historical_names.name: Vegium
historical_names.source: 1st century AD (Pliny's Naturalis Historia / Ptolemy)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Liburnian-Roman town of Vegium occupied the site of Bag/Karlobag.

b_udbina.first_mention_attestation: 1493 AD (first mentioned as Udbina at the Battle of Krbava Field; earlier Civitas Corbaviae 1185)
b_udbina.etymology_analysis: Earlier known as *Civitas Corbaviae* (seat of Bishop of Krbava from 1185 AD); first attested under the name *Udbina* in 1493 AD.

b_dreznik.first_mention_attestation: 1185 AD (first mentioned as Drežnik in 1185 AD)
b_dreznik.etymology_analysis: Medieval frontier fortress above the Korana river, first attested in 1185 AD.

b_modrus.first_mention_attestation: 1193 AD (granted to the Frankopan family by King Béla III)

morphemes.translation: blue-ish / dark hill or personal name

b_modrus.etymology_analysis: Medieval seat of the Frankopan family (Tržan Castle), first attested in 1193 AD.

b_okic.first_mention_attestation: 1193 AD (first mentioned in medieval Croatian sources)

morphemes.translation: fortress on a prominent peak (possibly from *ok- 'eye/lookout')

b_okic.etymology_analysis: Hilltop castle in the Samobor Hills, first attested in 1193 AD.

b_dubovac.first_mention_attestation: 1387 AD (late 14th century market town and castle)
b_dubovac.etymology_analysis: Named after the oak forest (*dubova šuma*) that surrounded it; first attested in the late 14th century (1387 AD).

b_topusko.first_mention_attestation: 1192 AD (thermal resort under King Béla III / Andrew II; Roman Ad Fines)
b_topusko.etymology_analysis: Named after its volcanic thermal springs; medieval name Topusko attested from 1192 AD, on the site of Roman *Ad Fines*.

historical_names.name: Ad Fines
historical_names.source: 2nd–3rd century AD (Roman road station Ad Fines, Tabula Peutingeriana / Antonine Itinerary)
historical_names.notes: Roman thermal station Ad Fines occupied the site of Topusko.

b_sinjcroat.first_mention_attestation: 1341 AD (fortress Fsini / Vsinj; Cetina župa 949 AD)

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly from Roman *Osinium* or Slavic root

b_sinjcroat.etymology_analysis: First attested as *Fsini*/*Vsinj* in 1341 AD, gradually replacing *Cetina* (attested 949 AD in DAI). Near Roman colony *Aequum* (45 AD).

historical_names.name: Aequum
historical_names.source: c. 45 AD (Colonia Claudia Aequum founded under Emperor Claudius)
historical_names.notes: Roman colony Aequum (modern Čitluk near Sinj) was founded in the 1st century AD.

b_split.first_mention_attestation: c. 3rd century BC (Greek colony Aspálathos; Diocletian's Palace 305 AD)
b_split.etymology_analysis: From Greek *Aspálathos* (3rd c. BC) and Latin *Spalatum*, later centered on Diocletian's Palace (305 AD).

b_solin.first_mention_attestation: 119 BC (Roman Salona, conquered/allied; birthplace of Diocletian)
b_solin.etymology_analysis: Direct phonological descendant of ancient Delmataean/Roman *Salona* (attested 2nd century BC; capital of Roman Dalmatia).

b_knin.first_mention_attestation: 7 BC (Strabo's Geographica as Ninia; medieval Tinum)
b_knin.etymology_analysis: Attested by Strabo (7 BC) as *Ninia*; medieval Croatian royal stronghold (*Tinum* / *Knin*).

b_bribir.first_mention_attestation: c. 949 AD (župa Berbera in Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio)
b_bribir.etymology_analysis: Slavicized from Roman *Municipium Varvariae* (1st c. AD); the Slavic form *Berbera* (Bribir) is first attested in *De Administrando Imperio* (c. 949 AD).

historical_names.name: Varvaria
historical_names.source: 1st century AD (Roman Municipium Varvariae, Pliny / inscriptions)
historical_names.notes: Roman Municipium Varvariae occupied Bribirska glavica in antiquity.

historical_names.name: Municipium Varvariae
historical_names.source: 1st century AD (Roman Municipium Varvariae, Pliny / inscriptions)
historical_names.notes: Roman Municipium Varvariae occupied Bribirska glavica in antiquity.

b_sibenik.first_mention_attestation: 1066 AD (Christmas charter of King Petar Krešimir IV)
b_sibenik.etymology_analysis: First attested on Christmas 1066 AD in a charter of King Petar Krešimir IV; traditionally linked to *šiba* ('twig/palisade') or Illyrian root.

b_zadar.first_mention_attestation: 384 BC (Greek inscription from Pharos mentioning Iadasinoi / Iadera)
b_zadar.etymology_analysis: From Pre-Indo-European / Liburnian *Iadera* (attested 384 BC), yielding Dalmatian *Jadra* / Italian *Zara* / Croatian *Zadar*.

b_nin.first_mention_attestation: 4th century BC (Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax as Hemionoi/Ainona; Roman Aenona)
b_nin.etymology_analysis: From Liburnian *Ainona* / Roman *Aenona* (4th century BC), becoming Croatian *Nin* and the first Croatian bishopric (9th c. AD).

b_biograd.first_mention_attestation: c. 949 AD (Belgradon in Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio)
b_biograd.etymology_analysis: Croatian 'White Town on the Sea' (Latin *Alba Maritima*); first attested c. 949 AD in *De Administrando Imperio* as *Belgradon*.

b_obrovac.first_mention_attestation: 1337 AD (first mentioned as Obrouec under the Kurjaković family)
b_obrovac.etymology_analysis: From Croatian *obrov* ('trench/earthwork'); first attested in 1337 AD as *Obrouec*.

b_soli.first_mention_attestation: 950 AD: attested as 'Salines' (Greek: Σαλῆνες, rendering Slavic 'Soli') in Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio.

morphemes.translation: salts (plural of sol, referring to salt springs/deposits)

b_soli.etymology_analysis: Medieval Slavic 'Soli' ('salts', rendered in Greek as 'Salines' in 950 AD) refers to the rich subterranean salt deposits and brine springs at the site. Under Ottoman rule from the 16th century, it was translated into Ottoman Turkish 'Tuzla' ('saltworks / place of salt').

b_bijeljina.first_mention_attestation: 1446 AD: first reliably attested on 3 March 1446 in a Dubrovnik (Ragusan) archival document regarding a merchant robbed near Bijeljina.

morphemes.translation: white (from Proto-Slavic *bělъ, referring to white sandy Drina deposits or a personal/estate root)

b_bijeljina.etymology_analysis: Derived from the South Slavic root 'bijel-' ('white', either referring to the light-colored sandy alluvial soil of the Drina/Semberija plain or an early Slavic personal name/estate *Bělinъ) with the toponymic suffix '-jina'.

b_zvornik.first_mention_attestation: 1410 AD: first mentioned on 21 May 1410 in a Dubrovnik (Ragusan) document as 'Zvonik' ('bell tower'); the modern form 'Zvornik' is attested from 1519.

morphemes.translation: noun/place suffix (zvonik = 'bell tower', later epenthetic -r- > Zvornik)

b_zvornik.etymology_analysis: Originally attested as 'Zvonik' ('bell tower', reportedly after the bell tower of a Franciscan monastery or a prominent watchtower), later undergoing epenthesis of '-r-' (folk-etymologically or phonetically) to 'Zvornik' by 1519.

b_srebrenik.first_mention_attestation: 1333 AD: first attested on 15 February 1333 in the charter of Bosnian Ban Stephen II Kotromanić to Dubrovnik (Ragusa).
b_srebrenik.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'srebro' ('silver') + '-enik', denoting a fortified town or settlement associated with silver mining, minting, or silvery limestone cliffs.

b_usora.first_mention_attestation: 1244 AD: first mentioned on 20 July 1244 in a papal/royal bull of King Béla IV of Hungary as 'Vozora' ('decimas in Vozora, in Sou...').

morphemes.translation: eponymous river name (likely of pre-Slavic/Illyrian hydronymic origin, Latinized as Vozora)

b_usora.etymology_analysis: Named after the Usora River (a left tributary of the Bosna), which gave its name to the medieval Bosnian land (zemlja) and župa of Usora, first documented as 'Vozora' in 1244.

b_maglaj.first_mention_attestation: 1408 AD: first officially mentioned on 18 September 1408 in a charter of King Sigismund of Hungary as 'Sub castro nostro Maglay'.
b_maglaj.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'magla' ('fog, mist'), referring to the frequent river mists rising from the Bosna valley around the steep fortress rock.

b_tolisa.first_mention_attestation: 1244 AD: first mentioned in a 1244 charter of King Béla IV of Hungary as 'Terra Tolis' (territory along the Tolisa River in Usora).

morphemes.translation: eponymous river name (right tributary of the Sava)

b_tolisa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tolisa River, a right tributary of the Sava in Bosnian Posavina; the territory around the river is first recorded as 'Terra Tolis' in 1244.

b_vodicevo.first_mention_attestation: 1197 AD: County Vodice and Vodičevo ('Wodicha') are first mentioned in charters of 1197 and 1200 granted by King Emeric of Hungary to Stephen I Babonić.
b_vodicevo.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'vodica' ('small stream/water', from 'voda' + '-ica') with the possessive/toponymic suffix '-evo', reflecting the Vodičevo stream and medieval župa Vodica.

b_dubica.first_mention_attestation: 1197 AD: first mentioned in historical sources in 1197 (and as 'castrum Dobicha' in 1258) on the right bank of the Una River.
b_dubica.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'dub' ('oak tree') + '-ica', denoting an oak forest or settlement by oak woods (the modern prefix 'Kozarska' refers to Mount Kozara, replacing 'Bosanska' after 1992).

b_banjaluka.first_mention_attestation: 1494 AD: first mentioned on 6 February 1494 in a charter issued by King Ladislaus II of Hungary.

morphemes.translation: of the ban (possessive adjective from title 'ban', or 'bath/spa' in folk etymology)

b_banjaluka.etymology_analysis: Interpreted as 'the Ban's meadow' (from the medieval South Slavic/Croatian-Bosnian title 'ban' + 'luka' meaning 'river meadow/valley'), though popular etymology also links it to 'banja' ('thermal bath').

b_gradiska.first_mention_attestation: 1295 AD: first mentioned in 1295 (and as 'Gradiški Brod' in 1330) as a Sava river crossing.
b_gradiska.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'grad' ('fortress, town') + '-iška', referring to the site of an earlier fortified settlement (the Roman river port and station Servitium).

historical_names.name: Servitium
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD, as Serbinon) and Itinerarium Antonini / Tabula Peutingeriana (as Servitium)
historical_names.notes: Roman river port and military/road station on the Sava at modern Gradiška.

historical_names.name: Serbinon
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD, as Serbinon) and Itinerarium Antonini / Tabula Peutingeriana (as Servitium)
historical_names.notes: Roman river port and military/road station on the Sava at modern Gradiška.

historical_names.name: Serbinum
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD, as Serbinon) and Itinerarium Antonini / Tabula Peutingeriana (as Servitium)
historical_names.notes: Roman river port and military/road station on the Sava at modern Gradiška.

b_glaz.first_mention_attestation: 1244 AD: first mentioned in 1244 as a fortified town ('Glaz') where King Béla IV of Hungary stayed.

morphemes.translation: medieval fort/župa name of uncertain origin (possibly from *glaž 'glass' or Slavic *glazъ)

b_glaz.etymology_analysis: Medieval Bosnian/Slavonian fortified town and župa seat on the border of Usora whose exact location and etymology remain uncertain (possibly linked to Kajkavian/Slavic 'glaž' or a personal/topographic root).

b_ragusa.first_mention_attestation: c. 700 AD: first attested as 'Ragusium' in the Ravenna Cosmography (Geographia Ravennatis 4.16: 'Epitaurum id est Ragusium'), and besieged 866–867 AD.

morphemes.translation: rocky island, cliff (from Greek λᾶας / Romance *lausa, giving Rausium > Ragusium > Ragusa)

b_ragusa.etymology_analysis: Founded in the 7th century on a rocky islet ('Lausa') by refugees from Epidaurum; 'Lausa' evolved via rhotacism/hypercorrection to 'Rausium', 'Ragusium', and 'Ragusa'. The Slavic name 'Dubrovnik' (first recorded 1189) derives from Proto-Slavic *dǫbrava ('oak grove').

b_ston.first_mention_attestation: 877 AD: the Diocese of Ston ('Stagnum') is first attested in 877 AD (and later as 'Stamnum' in Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio, c. 950 AD).

morphemes.translation: still water, lagoon, pond (giving Stamnum > Ston in South Slavic)

b_ston.etymology_analysis: Derived from Latin 'stagnum' ('still water, lagoon', referring to the shallow salt-pan bay at the Pelješac isthmus), adapted into Dalmatian Romance and South Slavic as 'Stamnum' > 'Ston'.

b_pozega.first_mention_attestation: c. 1196 AD: first mentioned as 'Posega' in the Gesta Hungarorum (late 12th c.), with Požega County attested in 1210 and the town in a 1227 charter of Andrew II.

morphemes.translation: burn, scorch (related to požar 'forest fire' / žega 'heat')

b_pozega.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic *požega (related to 'požar' 'forest fire' / 'žega' 'intense heat'), likely referring to slash-and-burn forest clearing in the Požega Valley.

historical_names.name: Incerum
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (Antonine Itinerary, c. 300 AD)
historical_names.notes: Roman road station Incerum was located in the Požega Basin (near Tekić/Vetovo) as the Roman predecessor settlement.

historical_names.name: Inicerum
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (Antonine Itinerary, c. 300 AD)
historical_names.notes: Roman road station Incerum was located in the Požega Basin (near Tekić/Vetovo) as the Roman predecessor settlement.

b_kutina.first_mention_attestation: 1256 AD: first mentioned in historical records in 1256.
b_kutina.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'kut' ('corner, secluded nook') + '-ina', or from the eponymous Kutinica stream, denoting a tucked-away settlement at the edge of Moslavina.

b_brod.first_mention_attestation: 1244 AD: traditionally cited as first mentioned as 'Brod' in a 1244 charter of King Béla IV (later 'Brod na Savi', renamed 'Slavonski Brod' in 1934).
b_brod.etymology_analysis: From Old Slavic 'brodъ' ('river ford'), referring to the strategic shallow crossing over the Sava River; the adjective 'Slavonski' was added in 1934.

historical_names.name: Marsonia
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD), Tabula Peutingeriana (4th c.), and Notitia Dignitatum
historical_names.notes: Roman fort and settlement Marsonia on the Sava road between Siscia and Sirmium.

historical_names.name: Marsonie
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD), Tabula Peutingeriana (4th c.), and Notitia Dignitatum
historical_names.notes: Roman fort and settlement Marsonia on the Sava road between Siscia and Sirmium.

b_vakovo.first_mention_attestation: c. 1196 AD: first mentioned as 'Vlco' in the Gesta Hungarorum (late 12th c.), and as 'Wolcou' / 'Vukovo' in 1220; Hungarian 'Vukovár' supplanted 'Vukovo' in the late 17th century.
b_vakovo.etymology_analysis: Means 'fortress on the Vuka River': originally Slavic 'Vukovo' / 'Vlkovo' (from the Vuka River, ancient 'Ulca'), later combined with Hungarian 'vár' ('fortress') to form 'Vukovár' / 'Vukovar'.

b_osijek.first_mention_attestation: 1196 AD: first mentioned in a 1196 charter of King Emeric of Hungary as 'Osijek' (Hungarian: 'Eszék').

natural_proper_name.name: Elevated dry bank above Drava marshes (oseka)

b_osijek.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'oseka' ('ebb tide, dry elevated ridge'), referring to the raised ground along the Drava River that protected the settlement from marshland flooding.

historical_names.name: Mursa
historical_names.source: Roman inscriptions / Emperor Hadrian elevation to Colonia Aelia Mursa (c. 133 AD; Ptolemy Geographia)
historical_names.notes: Major Celtic-Roman city and colony on the Drava at modern Osijek.

historical_names.name: Colonia Aelia Mursa
historical_names.source: Roman inscriptions / Emperor Hadrian elevation to Colonia Aelia Mursa (c. 133 AD; Ptolemy Geographia)
historical_names.notes: Major Celtic-Roman city and colony on the Drava at modern Osijek.

b_orahovica.first_mention_attestation: 1228 AD: first officially mentioned in 1228 in a charter issued by King Andrew II of Hungary.
b_orahovica.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'orah' ('walnut tree') + '-ovica', denoting a place or valley abundant in walnut trees.

b_krapina.first_mention_attestation: 1193 AD: first mentioned in 1193 by Kalán Bár-Kalán, Bishop of Pécs and Ban of Croatia and Dalmatia.
b_krapina.etymology_analysis: Named after the local river (Krapina / Krapinčica), derived from South Slavic 'krap' ('carp') + '-ina'.

b_garestin.first_mention_attestation: 1181 AD: first mentioned under its historical name 'Garestin' on 20 August 1181 in a legal charter of King Béla III of Hungary.

morphemes.translation: early medieval name of Varaždin (origin debated; later replaced by Varaždin from Hungarian Varasd: város 'city' + -d)

b_garestin.etymology_analysis: 'Garestin' (Guarestin) was the earliest recorded medieval name of Varaždin (1181), of uncertain/debated origin, before being superseded by 'Varaždin' (via Hungarian 'Varasd', from 'város' 'city' + diminutive '-d').

b_krizevci.first_mention_attestation: 1193 AD: first mentioned as 'Upper Križevac' in 1193 in a document of King Béla III of Hungary.
b_krizevci.etymology_analysis: Derived from Croatian 'križ' ('cross', referring to a church/monastery of the Holy Cross or a crossroads) + plural toponymic suffix '-evci'.

b_koprivnica.first_mention_attestation: 1272 AD: first mentioned in 1272 in a charter of Prince Ladislaus IV of Hungary.
b_koprivnica.etymology_analysis: Named after the local Koprivnica stream, derived from South Slavic 'kopriva' ('stinging nettle') + '-nica'.

b_verevce.first_mention_attestation: 1234 AD: first mentioned in 1234 as 'magna villa Wereuche' (Verevce / Verőce).

morphemes.translation: spring, whirlpool, or gate/faith (evolved via Wereuche > Verőce > Virovitica)

b_verevce.etymology_analysis: Attested in 1234 as 'Wereuche' (reflecting Slavic *Věrevьce / *Virjevcь, Hungarian 'Verőce'), later expanded with '-itica' to 'Virovitica'.

b_zagreb.first_mention_attestation: 1094 AD: first recorded in connection with the foundation of the Zagreb Diocese by King Ladislaus I in 1094 (and explicitly as 'Zagreb' in the 1134 charter of Felician, Archbishop of Esztergom).

morphemes.translation: embankment, hill, or riverbank (via metathesis *zabreg > zagreb)

b_zagreb.etymology_analysis: Derived from Proto-Slavic *zagrebъ ('embankment, behind the ridge/hill') or via metathesis from *zabregъ ('behind the Sava riverbank').

historical_names.name: Andautonia
historical_names.source: Ptolemy's Geographia (c. 150 AD) and Itinerarium Antonini
historical_names.notes: Roman municipium of Andautonia (modern Ščitarjevo, ~10 km southeast of Zagreb) was the Roman urban center of the Zagreb area (1st–5th c. AD).

b_cazma.first_mention_attestation: 1094 AD: first mentioned in 1094 when King Ladislaus I of Hungary granted Čazma to the newly founded Bishopric of Zagreb.

morphemes.translation: river name (Česma, tributary of the Lonja)

b_cazma.etymology_analysis: Named after the nearby Česma River (medieval 'Chasma' / 'Čazma').

b_samobor.first_mention_attestation: 1242 AD: first attested in 1242 when King Béla IV granted it the status of a free royal town.
b_samobor.etymology_analysis: Compound of South Slavic 'samo-' ('solitary, only') + 'bor' ('pine tree/forest'), meaning 'solitary pine' or 'pure pine forest'.

b_sisak.first_mention_attestation: 35 BC: attested as 'Siscia' (and Celtic-Illyrian 'Segestica') during Octavian's Illyrian campaign (Strabo, Pliny, Appian), and in 822 AD as 'Siscia' (seat of Duke Ljudevit Posavski in the Royal Frankish Annals).

morphemes.translation: ancient town name (direct phonological ancestor of Croatian Sisak)

b_sisak.etymology_analysis: Pre-Roman Celtic-Illyrian 'Segestica' / 'Siscia' (35 BC), which served as the Roman provincial capital of Pannonia Savia and early medieval Slavic seat of Duke Ljudevit (819–822 AD), evolving directly into Croatian 'Sisak'.

b_mokro.first_mention_attestation: 533 AD: attested as 'Muccurum' / 'Macrum' in the Acts of the Synod of Salona on 4 May 533 AD (and as 'Mokron' in De Administrando Imperio, c. 950 AD).

morphemes.translation: ancient settlement name adapted into Slavic as 'Mokro' (folk-etymologized with 'mokro' = wet) and 'Makar' > 'Makarska'

b_mokro.etymology_analysis: Late Antique 'Muccurum' / 'Macrum' (533 AD) was phonologically adapted by South Slavs as 'Mokro' (the administrative center of Narentine Paganija) and 'Makar', giving modern 'Makarska'.

b_omis.first_mention_attestation: 77 AD: attested as 'Oneum' in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (3.142) and 'Onaeum' in Ptolemy (c. 150 AD), evolving via Dalmatian Romance 'Almissum' / 'Olmissium' into 'Omiš'.

morphemes.translation: cliff/hill settlement (PIE *almissa 'cliff' or Illyrian-Greek Onaion) -> Slavic Omiš

b_omis.etymology_analysis: Roman-Illyrian 'Oneum' / 'Onaeum' (77 AD) and Late Latin 'Almissum' / 'Olmissium' evolved phonologically through Dalmatian Romance into Croatian 'Omiš'.

b_hvar.first_mention_attestation: 384 BC: founded as the Greek colony 'Pharos' (Φάρος) by colonists from Paros in 384 BC (recorded by Diodorus Siculus).

morphemes.translation: island/colony name (from Paros or Illyrian 'fara'), adapted via Dalmatian 'Fara' > Slavic 'Hvar'

b_hvar.etymology_analysis: Greek 'Pharos' (384 BC) passed through Latin 'Pharus' and Dalmatian Romance 'Fara' into Croatian 'Hvar' via the regular South Slavic substitution /f/ > /xv/ (> /hv/).

b_blagaj.first_mention_attestation: 950 AD: first attested as 'Bona' in Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio (c. 950 AD) as a town of Zachlumia; later named 'Blagaj'.

morphemes.translation: mild, gentle, blessed (referring to the mild climate)

b_blagaj.etymology_analysis: The medieval Slavic name 'Blagaj' derives from 'blag' ('mild, gentle'), referring to the mild Mediterranean-influenced microclimate at the Buna River spring; in c. 950 AD it was recorded as 'Bona'.

b_nevesinje.first_mention_attestation: 1219 AD: earliest preserved mention in the Annals of the Patriarchal Monastery of Peć in 1219 (also mentioned in the 12th-century Chronicle of the Priest of Duklja).

morphemes.translation: uncertain (folk-etymologized as 'ne-veselo' or from a pre-Slavic/personal root *Nevesin)

b_nevesinje.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1219; the name is formed with the South Slavic toponymic suffix '-inje', likely from an early Slavic personal name *Nevesinъ or a pre-Slavic substratum root.

b_drijeva.first_mention_attestation: 1186 AD: first mentioned as 'Drijeva' in a 1186 trade treaty between Serbian Grand Župan Stefan Nemanja and the Republic of Ragusa (with slave-market references from 1080).

morphemes.translation: wood, boat, ferry (referring to the river port/ferry on the Neretva)

b_drijeva.etymology_analysis: Medieval 'Drijeva' / 'Drijevo' derives from Old South Slavic *drěvo ('wood, wooden boat/ferry'), reflecting its role as a major Neretva river port and customs market; later renamed 'Gabela' (from Italian/Arabic 'gabella' = customs tax).

historical_names.name: Narona
historical_names.source: Pseudo-Scylax Periplus (4th century BC) and Roman sources (2nd century BC)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Illyrian-Roman emporium and colony of Narona (modern Vid, ~4 km from Gabela/Drijeva) was the direct predecessor port on the lower Neretva.

b_kljuc.first_mention_attestation: 1410 AD: first mentioned on 28 December 1410 in a charter of Bosnian Duke Sandalj Hranić Kosača.

morphemes.translation: key (metaphorical for a strategic mountain pass/stronghold controlling access)

b_kljuc.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic 'ključ' ('key'), a common medieval fortress name denoting a strategic stronghold that 'locks' or controls a mountain pass or trade route (here the Dubrovnik–Gacko–Drina route).

b_mostar.first_mention_attestation: 1452 AD: earliest documented reference to the settlement on 3 April 1452 in Ragusan records; first mentioned by the name 'Mostar' in an Ottoman document of 1474.
b_mostar.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'mostari' ('bridge-keepers', from 'most' 'bridge' + '-ar'), referring to the guards who tended the wooden suspension bridge over the Neretva before the Ottoman stone bridge.

b_hlivno.first_mention_attestation: 892 AD: first attested on 28 September 892 in the Charter of Croatian Duke Muncimir (witnessed by Želimir, župan of Livno / Cleuna), and as Χλεβίανα (Chlebiana) in De Administrando Imperio (c. 950).

morphemes.translation: early Slavic form *Chlěvьno / *Chlebiana (possibly from *chlěvъ 'shelter/stable' or pre-Slavic root)

b_hlivno.etymology_analysis: Medieval 'Hlivno' (892 AD 'Cleuna', c. 950 'Chlebiana') lost its initial 'h-' in standard Bosnian/Croatian to become 'Livno'.

historical_names.name: Pelva
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (Antonine Itinerary, c. 300 AD)
historical_names.notes: Roman road station Pelva on the Salona–Servitium road was situated in the Livno Field (Livanjsko polje).

b_glamoc.first_mention_attestation: 1078 AD: first mentioned in 1078 as 'Dlamoč' (a border župa of the Croatian Kingdom).
b_glamoc.etymology_analysis: Evolved from medieval 'Dlamoč' (1078) via dissimilation/alteration of 'dl-' > 'gl-' to 'Glamoč'; the root is linked to the Illyrian root *dalma/*delma ('sheep, pasture').

historical_names.name: Salvium
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 AD) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Roman municipium of Salvium (modern Vrba near Glamoč) was the Roman urban center of Glamočko Polje.

historical_names.name: Salviae
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Antonini (c. 300 AD) and Tabula Peutingeriana
historical_names.notes: Roman municipium of Salvium (modern Vrba near Glamoč) was the Roman urban center of Glamočko Polje.

b_duvno.first_mention_attestation: 167 BC: attested as Illyrian 'Delminium' (capital of the Dalmatae, conquered by Rome in 155 BC; bishopric attested in 591 AD), evolving via Late Latin *Delminio > Slavic 'Dumno' > 'Duvno'.
b_duvno.etymology_analysis: Illyrian-Roman 'Delminium' (from Illyrian *delma 'sheep/pasture') evolved phonologically via Late Antique *Delminio into South Slavic 'Dumno' and 'Duvno' (renamed 'Tomislavgrad' in 1928).

b_imotski.first_mention_attestation: c. 950 AD: first attested as 'Hemotha' / 'Imota' (Ζουπανία τὰ Ἤμοτα) in Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus's De Administrando Imperio.
b_imotski.etymology_analysis: Derived from the pre-Slavic/Illyrian toponym 'Emotha' / 'Imota' (first recorded c. 950 AD as the Croatian župa of Imota) with the South Slavic adjectival suffix '-ski'.

b_gacko.first_mention_attestation: 1276 AD: first mentioned in 1276 as the site of the Battle of Gacko between Serbian King Stefan Uroš I and his son Dragutin.

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly from *gatъ 'dyke/causeway' + -sko, or linked in folk/older historiography to Goths)

b_gacko.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1276; its name is formed with the Slavic neuter suffix '-sko' (often derived from *gatъ 'embankment/causeway' across the karst polje, or in older tradition from the Goths).

b_konjic.first_mention_attestation: 1382 AD: earliest recorded by name on 16 June 1382 in the archives of the Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik).
b_konjic.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'konj' ('horse') + '-ić', likely referring to a horse-changing station/caravan stop on the Neretva trade route between Herzegovina and central Bosnia.

b_obalj.first_mention_attestation: 1323 AD: the medieval župa of Zagorje (whose seat was the fortress of Obalj) is first mentioned c. 1322–1323 in a charter of Bosnian Ban Stephen II Kotromanić.
b_obalj.etymology_analysis: Derived from South Slavic 'obal' ('round, rounded'), describing the rounded hill or ridge on which the medieval fortress of Obalj (seat of župa Zagorje) stood.

b_buthrotum.first_mention_attestation: 6th century BCE (c. 500 BCE), attested as 'Bouthroton' (Βουθρωτόν) by Hecataeus of Miletus in his Periegesis.
b_buthrotum.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Βουθρωτόν (Bouthrōtón), Latinized as Buthrotum and evolving into Albanian Butrint. Classical tradition (Virgil, Servius) derives it from 'wounded bull' (boûs + trōtós), referring to a sacrificial bull that escaped and swam ashore.

b_corfu.first_mention_attestation: 10th century AD (c. 950–968 AD), attested via Medieval Greek 'Koryphō' (Κορυφώ) and Latinized in Western sources as 'Corfu'.

natural_proper_name.name: Koryphai (twin peaks of the Old Fortress)

b_corfu.etymology_analysis: The Western name Corfu derives via Venetian/Italian Corfù from Byzantine Greek Κορυφώ (Koryphṓ, 'city of the peaks'), referring to the twin peaks of the Palaio Frourio (Old Fortress) peninsula.

historical_names.name: Kerkyra
historical_names.source: Mycenaean Linear B 'ko-ro-ku-ra-i-jo' (c. 1300 BCE); Strabo/Herodotus as Korkyra.
historical_names.notes: Ancient and native Greek name is Kerkyra (Doric Korkyra), attested since the Mycenaean period.

historical_names.name: Scheria
historical_names.source: Mycenaean Linear B 'ko-ro-ku-ra-i-jo' (c. 1300 BCE); Strabo/Herodotus as Korkyra.
historical_names.notes: Ancient and native Greek name is Kerkyra (Doric Korkyra), attested since the Mycenaean period.

b_cephalonia.first_mention_attestation: 8th century BCE (c. 750 BCE), attested as 'Kephallēnes' (Κεφαλλῆνες) in Homer's Iliad (2.631) and Odyssey.
b_cephalonia.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Κεφαλληνία (Kephallēnía), named in Greek mythology after the Athenian hero Cephalus (or from the ethnonym Kephallēnes, meaning 'headlanders' or 'people of the head/promontory').

b_zakynthos.first_mention_attestation: c. 1300 BCE, attested in Mycenaean Linear B tablets at Pylos as 'za-ku-si-jo' (𐀼𐀓𐀯𐀍, 'man from Zakynthos'); later in Homer's Iliad (2.634).
b_zakynthos.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ζάκυνθος (Zákynthos), a Pre-Greek (Pelasgian) toponym characterized by the -nthos suffix (comparable to Korinthos, Erymanthos); Greek myth attributed it to an eponymous Arcadian hero Zakynthos.

b_antipatreia.first_mention_attestation: 217 BCE, attested as 'Antipatreia' (Ἀντιπάτρεια) in Polybius's Histories during the conflict between Skerdilaidas and Philip V of Macedon.
b_antipatreia.etymology_analysis: Antipatreia was founded/named in the Hellenistic period after Antipater (or his son Cassander's family); in the 9th century AD under the First Bulgarian Empire it received the Slavic name Beligrad ('White City'), which became Ottoman/Albanian Berat.

b_skrapar.first_mention_attestation: 1336 AD, first attested as the fortress 'Skreparion' (Σκρεπάριον) in the Byzantine chronicle of Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos.

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly linked to regional rocky/karst terrain or pre-Slavic root

b_skrapar.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1336 as Skreparion in John VI Kantakouzenos's chronicle (Ottoman İskarapar). The etymology is uncertain, though it refers to the mountainous region and fortress along the Osum canyon.

b_argyrokastron.first_mention_attestation: 1336 AD, first attested as 'Argyrokastron' (Ἀργυρόκαστρον) in the chronicle of Byzantine Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos.
b_argyrokastron.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Greek Ἀργυρόκαστρον (Argyrókastron, 'Silver Castle'), adapted into Albanian as Gjirokastër (Gheg Gjinokastër). Folk etymology linking it to Princess Argjiro is unhistorical.

b_kelycyre.first_mention_attestation: 1327 AD, attested as 'Clausura' (and 'Qlisura' in the 1432 Ottoman tax register).
b_kelycyre.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Greek κλεισοῦρα (kleisoûra, 'narrow pass/gorge') via Latin clausura, referring to the strategic Këlcyrë Gorge carved by the Vjosë River between Mount Trebeshinë and Mount Nemërçkë.

b_valamara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern written records; modern oronym Mali i Valamarës (Aromanian: Valea Mari).
b_valamara.etymology_analysis: Oronym of the Valamara massif in southeastern Albania (between the Shkumbin and Devoll rivers). Corresponding to Aromanian Valea Mari ('Great Valley'), reflecting Aromanian pastoral presence in the Pindus-Korçë highlands.

b_kruje.first_mention_attestation: 879–880 AD, first attested as Bishop David of 'Kroai' (Κροιῶν) in the acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople, and in Notitia 7 (c. 901–907).
b_kruje.etymology_analysis: Derived from Albanian krua (Proto-Albanian *krāna, 'spring, fountain'), rendered in Medieval Greek as Κροαί (Kroai). First attested in 879 AD, just after the 867 AD baseline.

historical_names.name: Albanopolis
historical_names.source: Ptolemy, Geography (c. 150 AD), as Ἀλβανόπολις (city of the Albanoi).
historical_names.notes: Albanopolis (identified with nearby Zgërdhesh) was the ancient Illyrian center of the Albanoi tribe in the Krujë region.

b_mat.first_mention_attestation: 4th–5th century AD (c. 400 AD), first attested as the river 'Mathis' by Roman geographer Vibius Sequester ('Mathis Dyrrachii, non longe a Lisso').
b_mat.etymology_analysis: Hydronym and region name derived from Proto-Albanian *mat ('elevated place', later shifting to 'riverbank/shore'). Attested in Late Antiquity as Mathis by Vibius Sequester.

b_lezhe.first_mention_attestation: 385 BCE, mentioned as 'Lissos' (Λισσός) in Diodorus Siculus (and 213 BCE in Polybius as Lissus/Acrolissus).
b_lezhe.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Λισσός (Lissós, 'smooth/sheer rock') and Latin Lissus, which evolved through regular Albanian sound changes into archaic Lesh and modern Lezhë.

b_hiskampis.first_mention_attestation: 333 AD, attested as 'Hiscampis' / 'Scampis' in the Itinerarium Burdigalense and Tabula Peutingeriana (following 2nd c. BCE Mansio Scampa).

morphemes.translation: crag, rock, or Roman station name (cf. Albanian shkëmb 'rock')

b_hiskampis.etymology_analysis: Hiscampis (Scampis) was the Late Roman/Early Byzantine fortress and bishopric on the Via Egnatia (possibly related to Illyrian/Albanian shkëmb 'rock/cliff'). Refounded in 1466 by Mehmed II as Ottoman İl-basan ('the fortress' > Elbasan).

b_avlonas.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (c. 150 AD), first attested as 'Aulon' (Αὐλών) by Ptolemy and Lucian.
b_avlonas.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Αὐλών (Aulṓn, 'channel/strait', referring to the Strait of Otranto), Latinized as Aulona, evolving into Medieval/Italian Valona and Albanian Vlorë.

b_himara.first_mention_attestation: 1st century AD (c. 77 AD), attested as 'Chimaera' (Χίμαιρα) by Pliny the Elder in Naturalis Historia (and later by Procopius in the 6th c. AD).
b_himara.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Χίμαιρα (Chímaira, Latin Chimaera), evolving into Albanian Himarë. Linguists connect it either to χείμαρρος ('mountain torrent') or an ancient coastal/hydronymic root.

b_debar.first_mention_attestation: 2nd century AD (c. 150 AD), attested as 'Deborus' (Δήβορος) in Ptolemy's Geography (and later in 11th c. AD by Basil II / Anna Komnena as Devre).
b_debar.etymology_analysis: Attested in Antiquity as Greek Δῆβορος / Latin Deborus (Ptolemy), continued as Byzantine Greek Δίβρη (Divre), South Slavic Debar, and Albanian Dibër (often associated with Slavic *dъbrъ 'valley/gorge' or a Paleo-Balkan root).

b_peshkopi.first_mention_attestation: 1020 AD, when the Dibër region was established as an episcopate (episkope) under the Archbishopric of Ohrid, centered at Peshkopi.
b_peshkopi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Medieval Greek ἐπισκοπή (episkopḗ, 'bishopric') and Albanian peshkop ('bishop', from Vulgar Latin *pescopus < episcopus), commemorating its 1020 AD elevation as an episcopal seat.

b_kukes.first_mention_attestation: 1571–1591 AD, first recorded in Ottoman tax registers (defters) of the Sanjak of Dukagjin.

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly from a personal/clan name or local root

b_kukes.etymology_analysis: First attested in late 16th-century Ottoman defters (1571–1591) as a small settlement at the confluence of the White and Black Drin; its etymology remains uncertain.

b_dyracchion.first_mention_attestation: 229 BCE (and 4th–3rd c. BCE coins reading ΔΥΡ), when Rome seized the city and adopted the name Dyrrhachium (Greek Dyrrhachion) over Epidamnos.
b_dyracchion.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Δυρράχιον (Dyrrháchion, 'difficult ridge/rocky shore'), Latinized as Dyrrhachium, evolving into Venetian Durazzo and Albanian Durrës.

historical_names.name: Epidamnos
historical_names.source: Founded c. 627 BCE by colonists from Corinth and Corcyra as Epidamnos (Ἐπίδαμνος).
historical_names.notes: Romans avoided 'Epidamnos' due to its resemblance to Latin damnum ('loss/harm'), preferring Dyrrhachium.

b_savra.first_mention_attestation: 1385 AD, attested as the plain/field of Savra in the Battle of Savra (18 September 1385) between Zeta and Ottoman-backed forces.

morphemes.translation: uncertain; local plain toponym near Lushnjë

b_savra.etymology_analysis: Savra (modern village Savër near Lushnjë) is first attested in 1385 AD as the site of the Battle of Savra; Lushnjë itself is first recorded in the 1431–1432 Ottoman defter.

b_naupaktos.first_mention_attestation: 5th century BCE (c. 455 BCE), attested as 'Naupaktos' (Ναύπακτος) in Thucydides (History of the Peloponnesian War).
b_naupaktos.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Ναύπακτος (Naúpaktos, 'shipyard/boatyard', from naûs 'ship' + pēg- 'to fasten'), later Venetian Lepanto and restored in modern Greece as Nafpaktos.

b_prousos.first_mention_attestation: 1845 AD, officially standardized as 'Prousos' (earlier 'Proussos' / 'Pyrsos' in Ottoman/early modern records; monastery icon tradition refers to 829–842 AD).
b_prousos.etymology_analysis: Named after the Monastery of Panagia Prousiotissa, whose icon was traditionally brought from Prusa (Bursa) in Bithynia during Iconoclasm (829–842 AD); the village itself is attested only in the early modern/modern period.

b_lidoriki.first_mention_attestation: 901–907 AD, first attested as the Bishopric of 'Loidorikion' (Λοιδορίκιον / Λιδωρίκιον) in the Notitia Episcopatuum of Emperor Leo VI the Wise.

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly linked to ancient Dorians (Doris) or a medieval personal/Slavic name

b_lidoriki.etymology_analysis: First attested in Leo VI's Notitia Episcopatuum (901–907 AD) as a suffragan bishopric of Larissa. Local tradition links it to the ancient Dorians of Doris, though its exact medieval etymology is debated.

b_ioaninna.first_mention_attestation: 879 AD, first attested as 'Ioannina' (Zacharias, Bishop of Ioannine) in the acts of the Fourth Council of Constantinople.

morphemes.translation: John (Saint John the Baptist or a founder/settler John)

b_ioaninna.etymology_analysis: Derived from the personal name Ioannes (attributed to a monastery of St. John the Baptist or a local founder) with the -ina suffix. First recorded in 879 AD, 12 years after the 867 AD baseline (Procopius's 6th-c. Euroea is a debated nearby predecessor).

b_konitsa.first_mention_attestation: 1380 AD, first attested in the Chronicle of Ioannina (Late Byzantine period).
b_konitsa.etymology_analysis: Most commonly derived from South Slavic *Konica ('horse place', from konjь 'horse' + -ica), though alternative theories link it to an ancient Epirote settlement Knossos/Konissos or a local lord Konis.

b_vella.first_mention_attestation: Mid-10th century AD (c. 950 AD), attested as 'Photice, that is Bela' (Φωτικῆς ἤτοι Βελᾶς) in the Byzantine Notitiae Episcopatuum.
b_vella.etymology_analysis: Of Slavic origin (cf. bělъ 'white'), attested from the mid-10th century as Bela (Βελᾶ), when the bishopric of ancient Photice was transferred to the fortified hill near modern Vella Monastery.

historical_names.name: Photice
historical_names.source: Hierocles, Synecdemus (c. 527 AD) and Procopius, De Aedificiis (6th c. AD).
historical_names.notes: The bishopric of Photice (in Thesprotia) was temporarily relocated to Bela in the 10th century.

b_grava.first_mention_attestation: Ottoman period / 1920 Greek census, attested as 'Grava' (Γράβα), the earlier name of Igoumenitsa until 1938.
b_grava.etymology_analysis: From Epirote Greek γράβα (gráva, 'cave/hollow'). Used as the name of the settlement of Igoumenitsa in Ottoman and early modern times until it was renamed Igoumenitsa in 1938.

b_metzovo.first_mention_attestation: 1380 AD, first attested as 'Metsovon' (Μέτσοβον) in the Chronicle of Ioannina.
b_metzovo.etymology_analysis: Generally derived from South Slavic *Mečkovo / *Medvedovo ('place of bears') or from Aromanian/Slavic roots; first attested in 1380 AD in the Chronicle of Ioannina.

b_gardiki.first_mention_attestation: Post-Slavic medieval/Ottoman attestation; no pre-867 written record.
b_gardiki.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *gradьcь / *gordьcь ('small fortress/town', diminutive of gradъ), borrowed into Medieval Greek as Γαρδίκι (Gardíki). Common medieval toponym in Epirus and western Thessaly (e.g., Gardiki, Trikala).

b_vrestenitsa.first_mention_attestation: Ottoman/post-medieval attestation as Vrestenitsa (area attested from 1515 Korakos Bridge and 1697 Seltsos Monastery); renamed Piges in the 20th century.
b_vrestenitsa.etymology_analysis: From South Slavic *Brestenica (Брестеница, 'elm place', from brestъ 'elm'), Hellenized as Βρεστενίτσα (Vrestenitsa), and later renamed Piges ('springs').

b_agrafa.first_mention_attestation: 1525 AD, recognized in the Ottoman treaty of Tamasi (1525) granting autonomy to the 'unwritten' mountain villages of Agrafa.
b_agrafa.etymology_analysis: From Greek Ἄγραφα (Ágrapha, literally 'unwritten'), referring to the remote Pindus mountain region omitted from Ottoman tax registers because the Ottomans could not subjugate its inhabitants.

b_arta.first_mention_attestation: 1082 AD, first attested as 'Arta' (Ἄρτα) during the Norman siege by Bohemond of Taranto.

morphemes.translation: debated: possibly from Arachthos river, Latin artus ('narrow'), or Slavic balta ('swamp')

b_arta.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1082 AD as Arta; its etymology is debated (variously linked to a corruption of the Arachthos River, Latin artus 'narrow', or Slavic balta 'marsh').

historical_names.name: Ambracia
historical_names.source: Founded c. 625 BCE as a Corinthian colony (Ambracia / Ἀμβρακία); capital of Pyrrhus of Epirus in 294 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Modern Arta stands directly on the site of ancient Ambracia.

b_sivista.first_mention_attestation: Ottoman/modern attestation; village in Agrafa (Evrytania) with church of Agia Marina built in 1900–1904 and no pre-867 written record.
b_sivista.etymology_analysis: Small mountain settlement in Agrafa (Evrytania) near the Achelous River / Lake Kremasta. Its name is likely of medieval Slavic or local origin, unattested before the Ottoman/modern era.

b_angelokastron.first_mention_attestation: 1294 AD, first attested when Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas gave it as dowry to Philip I of Taranto (called 'Gello Castro' in the Livre de la Conqueste).

eponym.details: Named after the Byzantine Angelos (Komnenos Doukas) dynasty that founded the Despotate of Epirus in the 13th century.

b_angelokastron.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Greek Ἀγγελόκαστρον (Angelókastron, 'Castle of Angelos'), built in the 13th century by the Despots of Epirus of the Angelos-Komnenos-Doukas house.

historical_names.name: Konope
historical_names.source: Polybius & Strabo (10.2.22); ancient Aetolian Konope renamed Arsinoe c. 299–281 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Ancient Konope/Arsinoe lay immediately adjacent to modern Angelokastro.

historical_names.name: Arsinoe
historical_names.source: Polybius & Strabo (10.2.22); ancient Aetolian Konope renamed Arsinoe c. 299–281 BCE.
historical_names.notes: Ancient Konope/Arsinoe lay immediately adjacent to modern Angelokastro.

b_vonitsa.first_mention_attestation: Early 10th century AD (c. 901 AD), first mentioned in Byzantine ecclesiastical/written sources as the seat of a bishop.
b_vonitsa.etymology_analysis: Prevailingly derived from South Slavic *Vodica / *Vodenica (from voda 'water', referring to the abundant coastal waters/springs on the Ambracian Gulf), first attested in the early 10th century.

historical_names.name: Anaktorion
historical_names.source: Founded c. 630 BCE by Corinthian colonists (Thucydides, Strabo).
historical_names.notes: Ancient Anaktorion stood immediately adjacent to Vonitsa on the southern shore of the Ambracian Gulf.

b_benevento.first_mention_attestation: 268 BC (Roman colony Beneventum, renamed from Maleventum)
b_benevento.etymology_analysis: Originally Samnite/Oscan Malies/Maloenton (Latinized as Maleventum), auspiciously renamed Beneventum by the Romans in 268 BC upon founding a Latin colony.

historical_names.name: Maleventum
historical_names.source: 275 BC (Battle of Maleventum; Livy / Polybius)
historical_names.notes: Pre-268 BC Samnite/Oscan name Maleventum, renamed Beneventum after the Roman victory over Pyrrhus.

historical_names.name: Maloenton
historical_names.source: 275 BC (Battle of Maleventum; Livy / Polybius)
historical_names.notes: Pre-268 BC Samnite/Oscan name Maleventum, renamed Beneventum after the Roman victory over Pyrrhus.

b_alife.first_mention_attestation: 326 BC (Samnite Allifae captured by Romans, Livy)

morphemes.translation: ancient Samnite settlement name (possibly related to *albh- 'white' or personal name)

b_alife.etymology_analysis: From Oscan/Samnite Allifae, attested during the Second Samnite War (326 BC) and later a Roman municipium.

morphemes.translation: sacred / divine (cf. Oscan aisusis) or hydronymic root

b_isernia.etymology_analysis: From Samnite/Roman Aesernia (Latin colony 263 BC), likely connected to Italic *ais- ('sacred') or a local Samnite place name.

b_melfi.first_mention_attestation: 1018 AD (fortified by Byzantine Catepan Basil Boioannes)
b_melfi.etymology_analysis: Named after the nearby Melfia stream (linked to Pliny's Melphes). First documented as a fortified town in 1018 AD under Byzantine Catepan Basil Boioannes.

b_ariano.first_mention_attestation: 892 AD (castrum Ariani, Lombard stronghold against Byzantines)
b_ariano.etymology_analysis: Predial toponym from Latin *praedium Arianum* ('estate of Arius'). Earliest written mention as *castrum Ariani* dates to 892 AD.

morphemes.translation: ancient Daunian city (linked by ancient etymology to lucus 'sacred grove' or Etruscan/Illyrian root)

b_lucera.etymology_analysis: Ancient Daunian city of Luceria, colonized by Rome in 314 BC.

b_larino.first_mention_attestation: 217 BC (Larinum, Livy XXII.18 during Second Punic War)

morphemes.translation: pre-Roman / Oscan settlement name (cf. Etruscan/Italic lar 'lord/hearth')

b_larino.etymology_analysis: From ancient Frentanian/Roman Larinum, attested in Livy during the Second Punic War (217 BC).

b_vieste.first_mention_attestation: 1002 AD (landing of Venetian Doge Pietro II Orseolo)

morphemes.translation: uncertain; traditionally linked to a temple of Vesta or Apeste

b_vieste.etymology_analysis: First attested in 1002 AD during Doge Pietro II Orseolo's naval expedition. Traditional etymology links it to Roman Vesta.

b_cosenza.first_mention_attestation: 356 BC (Consentia, capital of the Bruttii, Strabo / Livy)

morphemes.translation: agreement / confluence (of rivers Crati and Busento)

b_cosenza.etymology_analysis: Ancient Bruttian capital Consentia (4th century BC), Latinized as 'agreement' or confluence of the Crati and Busento rivers.

b_castrovillari.first_mention_attestation: 1064 AD (first attested as Castrum Villarum in medieval Norman historiography during Robert Guiscard's campaigns in northern Calabria, with secure charters from 1090–1094 AD under Roger Borsa)

morphemes.translation: of the villas / rural estates (genitive plural of villa)

b_castrovillari.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Latin 'Castrum Villarum' ('fortress of the villas/villages'), denoting the hilltop stronghold in Cosenza, Calabria, Italy, first attested in 11th-century Norman sources.

b_belvedere.first_mention_attestation: 1091 AD (carved date on portal of Chiesetta del Rosario)
b_belvedere.etymology_analysis: Descriptive Italian topographic name meaning 'beautiful view'. Earliest local attestation is the 1091 AD portal inscription on the Chiesetta del Rosario.

b_reggio_calabria.first_mention_attestation: c. 730 BC (Chalcidian Greek colony Rhegion, Strabo / Thucydides)
b_reggio_calabria.etymology_analysis: Founded c. 730 BC as Greek Rhegion; either from Greek *rhēgnymi* ('to break', referring to the Strait of Messina) or Italic *rēg-* ('royal').

b_squilluce.first_mention_attestation: c. 5th century BC (Greek Skylletion / Latin Scylacium, Strabo / Pliny)
b_squilluce.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Skylletion and Roman Scolacium / Scylacium, attested from the Classical Greek period.

b_tropea.first_mention_attestation: c. 6th century AD (Byzantine episcopal see / castrum Tropaea; Roman Portus Herculis nearby)
b_tropea.etymology_analysis: From Greek *tropaia* ('alternating wind' or 'trophies'), attested as an early Byzantine coastal stronghold and bishopric by the 6th–7th century AD.

b_rossano.first_mention_attestation: c. 3rd century AD (Roscianum in the Antonine Itinerary; Procopius 6th c.)
b_rossano.etymology_analysis: From Latin *Roscianum* ('estate of Roscius'), recorded in the 3rd-century Antonine Itinerary and by Procopius as a strong Byzantine fortress.

b_cotrone.first_mention_attestation: c. 710 BC (Achaean Greek colony Kroton, Herodotus / Strabo)
b_cotrone.etymology_analysis: Founded c. 710 BC by Achaean Greeks as Kroton (Latin Croto/Crotona).

b_catanzaro.etymology_analysis: Founded by the Byzantines in the early 10th century (attested c. 903 AD as Katantzárion / Arabic Qaṭanṣār).

b_capua.first_mention_attestation: 856 AD (New Capua founded by Lombard Count Lando on site of Casilinum)

morphemes.translation: uncertain; traditionally linked to Capys or Etruscan 'falcon' (capys)

b_capua.etymology_analysis: Modern Capua was founded in 856 AD on the site of Roman Casilinum (attested 216 BC), inheriting the name of ancient Capua (5 km southeast).

historical_names.name: Casilinum
historical_names.source: 216 BC (Siege of Casilinum, Livy XXIII.17)
historical_names.notes: Roman river port of Casilinum occupied the exact site of modern Capua before 856 AD.

b_gaeta.first_mention_attestation: 345 BC (Roman incorporation of Auruncan coast; Caieta in Strabo / Virgil)

morphemes.translation: hollow / gulf (Strabo) or nurse of Aeneas

b_gaeta.etymology_analysis: Ancient Caieta, linked by Strabo to Doric Greek *kaiata* ('hollow/cove'); fortified as a Byzantine castrum by the 6th century AD.

b_cassino.first_mention_attestation: 312 BC (Roman Casinum; Varro cites Oscan cascum 'ancient')
b_cassino.etymology_analysis: From Roman Casinum (from Oscan *cascum*, 'ancient' per Varro). Abbey of Montecassino founded above it c. 529 AD.

b_napoli.first_mention_attestation: c. 470 BC (Greek Neapolis 'New City', founded by Cumaeans)
b_napoli.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek Neapolis (Νεάπολις, 'New City'), founded in the 5th century BC alongside older Parthenope.

historical_names.name: Parthenope
historical_names.source: c. 680 BC (Cumaean Greek settlement Parthenope)
historical_names.notes: Earlier 7th-century BC Cumaean settlement Parthenope (later Palaepolis) immediately preceded Neapolis.

b_amalfi.first_mention_attestation: 596 AD (letter of Pope Gregory I mentioning Amalfi)

morphemes.translation: Roman gens Amarfia or refugees from Melfi

b_amalfi.etymology_analysis: Attested in 596 AD in a letter of Pope Gregory I; derived from the Roman gens Amarfia or legendary refugees from Melfi.

b_aversa.first_mention_attestation: 1030 AD (County of Aversa founded by Norman Rainulf Drengot)

morphemes.translation: local place name (Sancti Pauli ad Averze)

b_aversa.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1030 AD by the Norman leader Rainulf Drengot around the rural hamlet *Sancti Pauli ad Averze*.

b_camarda.first_mention_attestation: 1099 AD (first documentary mention of village Camarda)

morphemes.translation: hut / vaulted shelter (cf. Greek kamara) or local place name

b_camarda.etymology_analysis: Medieval village of Camarda (renamed Bernalda in 1470), first attested in a document of 1099 AD.

b_stigliano.first_mention_attestation: 1070 AD (donated to the Bishop of Tricarico)
b_stigliano.etymology_analysis: From Latin *Hostilianum* ('estate of Hostilius'). First documented in 1070 AD when donated to the Bishop of Tricarico.

b_salerno.etymology_analysis: From Roman Salernum (colony founded 194 BC), incorporating the pre-Roman root *sal-* ('sea/salt').

b_maratea.first_mention_attestation: 1079 AD (Marathia in a bull of Archbishop Alfano I of Salerno)
b_maratea.etymology_analysis: From Greek *marathos* ('wild fennel'), first attested in writing as *Marathia* in 1079 AD.

b_potenza.etymology_analysis: From Latin *Potentia* ('power'), established as a Roman municipium in Lucania in the 2nd century BC.

b_policastro.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek *Polykastron* ('many castles'), renamed in the 7th century AD on the site of ancient Greek Pyxous (471 BC) and Roman Buxentum.

historical_names.name: Pyxous
historical_names.source: 471 BC (Greek colony Pyxous founded by Rhegion; Roman Buxentum 194 BC)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek Pyxous / Roman Buxentum preceded the 7th-century Byzantine name Polykastron.

historical_names.name: Buxentum
historical_names.source: 471 BC (Greek colony Pyxous founded by Rhegion; Roman Buxentum 194 BC)
historical_names.notes: Ancient Greek Pyxous / Roman Buxentum preceded the 7th-century Byzantine name Polykastron.

b_mestre.first_mention_attestation: 994 AD: 'inter Mester et Paureliano et Brentulo' in a diploma of Emperor Otto III granting lands to Rambaldo, Count of Collalto (an uncertain 710 AD mention of 'Mestrina presso le montagne' is not securely identified with Mestre).

morphemes.translation: Roman personal name (gentilicium), or alternatively hydronym Mestria

b_mestre.etymology_analysis: According to Dante Olivieri, Mestre derives from the Roman personal name Mestrius (compare Mestrino near Padua and Mestrianis in Pannonia). Alternative hypotheses derive it from a local river Mestria or a pre-Roman root.

historical_names.name: Ad Nonum
historical_names.source: Itinerarium Burdigalense (333 AD): 'mutatio ad nonum', a Roman post-station nine miles from Altinum along the Via Annia.
historical_names.notes: Roman road station attested in the Mestre area prior to the medieval settlement of Mestre (first securely attested in 994 AD).

b_chioggia.first_mention_attestation: c. 77 AD: 'fossa Clodia' in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (III.121); later attested as Clodia, Cluza, and Clugia from the 6th century AD.
b_chioggia.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Latin hydronym Fossa Clodia (attested by Pliny the Elder), referring to a Roman navigable canal in the southern Venetian lagoon; phonologically evolved through Clodia > Cluza > Clugia > Chiozza > Chioggia.

b_malamacco.first_mention_attestation: 840 AD: 'Madamaucum' in the Pactum Lotharii (later Metamaucus and Mathemauco; served as ducal capital of Venice 742–810 AD per medieval chronicles).

morphemes.translation: ancient name of the Brenta river

b_malamacco.etymology_analysis: Dante Olivieri derives Madamaucum/Metamaucum from Maior Meduacus, the ancient name of the Brenta river that emptied into the lagoon nearby, evolving through Mamedòc- and Mademòc- into Malamocco (an older hypothesis by Bellemo proposed Greek μετὰ Μεδόα).

b_venezia.first_mention_attestation: 6 AD: 'Venetia' (Regio X Venetia et Histria) in the Augustan administrative division of Italy; later Byzantine 'Venetikà' / 'Venetia maritima' and plural 'Venetiae' for the lagoon city.
b_venezia.etymology_analysis: Named after the ancient Adriatic Veneti; originally the choronym Venetia for the mainland region (6 AD), then applied under Byzantine rule to the coastal lagoon (Venetia maritima / Venetikà) and in the plural Venetiae to the island city itself.

b_padua.first_mention_attestation: 141 BC: 'Patavini' in a Roman boundary inscription (CIL I² 633) adjudicating borders between Este and Padua; also Patavium in Polybius (2nd c. BC), Livy, and Pliny.

morphemes.translation: open, flat plain (or linked to Padus, Po river)

b_padua.etymology_analysis: From Roman Patavium (which shifted in Late Antiquity to Padua / Italian Padova). Likely formed from the IE root *pat- ('open plain') or the river name Padus, with the Venetic riverine suffix -av- (referring to the Brenta/Medoacus) and Latin -ium.

b_lonigo.first_mention_attestation: 1046 AD: cited as 'Leonicus' (and later 'Lunico') in medieval documents.
b_lonigo.etymology_analysis: A Roman predial toponym formed from the Latin personal name Leo plus the belonging suffix -īcus (Leonicus > Lunico > Lonigo). Although Roman settlers were present in the area from the 2nd century BC, the toponym is first attested in 1046 AD.

b_montagnana.first_mention_attestation: 996 AD: cited as a 'castrum' (Montagnana / Castrum Montanianae) in a document of 996 AD.

morphemes.translation: mansio / waystation name (or predial from Montanius + -ana)

b_montagnana.etymology_analysis: Traditionally derived from the Latin toponym Motta Aeniana (medieval Latin motta 'small elevation' + aeniana 'mansio') or a Roman predial form Montaniana; first attested as a castrum in 996 AD.

b_este.first_mention_attestation: 141 BC: 'Atestini' in a Roman boundary inscription (CIL I² 633) adjudicating borders between Este and Padua; later 'Ateste' in Pliny (NH III.130) and Tacitus.
b_este.etymology_analysis: From Latin Ateste, a Venetic toponym derived from the hydronym Athesis (the Adige river, which flowed past the town until the 589 AD Rotta della Cucca) plus the locative suffix -este.

b_rovigo.first_mention_attestation: 838 AD (April 24): 'villa que nuncupatur Rodigo' (Rodigium / Rhodigium) in a document from Ravenna.

morphemes.translation: Germanic personal name (modern scholarly etymology; folk etymology linked to Greek rhodon 'rose')

b_rovigo.etymology_analysis: First attested as Rodigo in 838 AD (later Rudi, Ruuigo); modern scholarship connects it to the Germanic personal name Hrodico, whereas Renaissance erudites derived Rhodigium from Greek rhodon ('rose').

b_adria.first_mention_attestation: c. 500 BC (6th century BC): 'Atria' / 'Adria' attested by Hecataeus of Miletus (cited by Stephanus of Byzantium); later 'Hatria'/'Atria' in Livy and Pliny.
b_adria.etymology_analysis: Ancient Etruscan-Venetic-Greek emporion that gave its name to the Adriatic Sea. Attested from the 6th century BC, its name is linked either to the ancient Po delta branch Adria or to a Venetic/Illyrian root adur ('water, sea').

b_treviso.first_mention_attestation: c. 77 AD: 'ex montibus Tarvisanis' in Pliny the Elder's Naturalis Historia (III.126); directly as 'Tarvisus' in Venantius Fortunatus (6th c. AD) and 'Tarvisium' in Paul the Deacon.

morphemes.translation: Celtic toponymic formant -is- + Latin neuter ending -ium

b_treviso.etymology_analysis: From Roman Tarvisium, most probably of Celtic origin: Gaulish tarvos ('bull') + the characteristic Gallic toponymic formant -is- + Latin -ium (a folk etymology instead links it to Latin ter-visi 'three hills').

b_ceneta.first_mention_attestation: c. 575 AD (6th century): 'Cenetam' in Venantius Fortunatus's De vita S. Martini (also 'Keneta' in Agathias, 6th c., and 'Ceneta'/'Cenita' in Paul the Deacon).

morphemes.translation: pre-Roman (likely Celtic) toponym of uncertain meaning

b_ceneta.etymology_analysis: Attested from the 6th century AD as Ceneta/Keneta, suggesting a pre-Roman (likely Celtic) origin of uncertain etymology; merged with Serravalle in 1866 to form Vittorio Veneto.

b_vicenza.first_mention_attestation: 135 BC: 'Veicetinos' (ethnonym) in a Roman boundary inscription (CIL I² 634) between Este and Vicenza; later 'Vicetia' in Pliny (NH III.130) and Tacitus.
b_vicenza.etymology_analysis: A Venetic formation from PIE *weik- ('settlement, village', cognate with Latin vicus) with the Venetic suffix -et- (seen in Veneti), yielding Roman Vicetia / Vicentia > medieval Vicencia > Vicenza.

b_verona.first_mention_attestation: c. 60 BC (mid-1st century BC): 'Verona' in Catullus (Carmina 35, 67, 68); also attested in Strabo (Geography V.1.6) and Pliny (NH III.130).

morphemes.translation: uncertain; possibly Celtic *werona 'enclosed territory' or water/alder root

b_verona.etymology_analysis: The exact etymology of Verona is uncertain; linguistic hypotheses link it to a Venetic or Celtic formation (e.g., Celtic *werona 'enclosed/defended territory' or *wern 'alder'), or an Indo-European water root.

b_lessinia.first_mention_attestation: 814 AD (May 7): 'Luxino' in a donation deed by gastald Ildemanno of Verona to the monastery of Santa Maria in Organo ('campo meo in Luxino ad Alpes facienda').

morphemes.translation: land used and prepared for mountain pastures (or from Veronese le sime 'peaks' / lisso 'log chute')

b_lessinia.etymology_analysis: Attested from 814 AD as Luxino (and later Lixino, Lesinio, Lissinorum, Lissinia), denoting highland pastureland; alternatively linked to Veronese le sime ('the peaks') or Venetian lisso ('timber slide').

b_garda.first_mention_attestation: 712 AD: 'Garda' attested in a document from the reign of Lombard King Liutprand (referring to the fortress/settlement on the Rocca di Garda).
b_garda.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Lombard/Germanic word warda ('place of guard, watchtower'), referring to the early medieval fortress on the Rocca di Garda; the settlement's name later replaced classical Benacus for Lake Garda.
